extracted.intended_audience: educational institutions (recipients of Federal financial assistance), Title IX coordinators, school administrators, institutional legal counsel, and compliance officers
extracted.subtask_description: Preamble to final Title IX regulations clarifying definitional and scope rules (e.g., 'recipient', 'student', 'party', and §106.11 application) and the standards a recipient must apply when addressing sex-based harassment and hostile environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'education program or activity' — fact-specific inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'education program or activity' is not separately defined in the Title IX statute or regulations, so a fact-specific inquiry is required to determine whether a particular program or activity of a non-educational institution recipient is educational, and thus covered by Title IX. Note that if any part of an educational institution receives Federal funds, all of its operations are covered by Title IX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat the inquiry as fact-specific; examples and case citations (e.g., O'Connor v. Davis; Horner; Cohen v. Brown Univ.) support broad coverage where federal funds are involved. The Department relies on the Civil Rights Restoration Act's clarification that 'program or activity' can encompass all operations when any part receives Federal funds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'recipient' — includes entities receiving funds directly or through an intermediary
rubrics_metrics.description: The longstanding regulatory definition of 'recipient' applies to entities that receive Federal assistance, whether directly or through an intermediary; this includes charter school operating companies and subcontractors engaged by charter schools when those entities receive Federal financial assistance through a contract with the intermediary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Department declines to amend §106.2 because courts have held such intermediated funding makes an entity a 'recipient' within Title IX. See Peltier v. Charter Day School and NCAA v. Smith. Institutions should treat contractors/subcontractors as recipients when they receive federal assistance directly or via an intermediary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'student' — 'a person who has gained admission'
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulation defines 'student' as 'a person who has gained admission,' a longstanding definition in effect since the original 1975 HEW regulations. This includes applicants who have gained admission even if they do not ultimately enroll.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department rejects claims this is overly burdensome; it expects recipients to notify admitted students of nondiscrimination policies and resolve complaints. 'Admission' is defined broadly in §106.2 to include selection for 'part-time, full-time, special, associate, transfer, exchange, or any other enrollment, membership, or matriculation.' The definition is intentionally not narrowed to match FERPA or Clery Act terminology because those statutes have different purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'party' — limited to complainant or respondent
rubrics_metrics.description: Final §106.2 defines 'party' as 'a complainant or respondent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'party' does not include a Title IX Coordinator who initiates a complaint under §106.44(f)(1)(v) or other participants in Title IX grievance procedures such as witnesses or adjudicators. This is a clarification of scope for procedural terms in the regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to defining 'sex discrimination' — rely on §106.10 and examples elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declined to add an explicit standalone definition of 'sex discrimination' to the regulations and instead relies on final §106.10 to clarify scope, with additional examples of prohibited sex discrimination provided in other sections including §106.31.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should use §106.10 and the examples in related sections (e.g., §106.31) to determine whether particular conduct constitutes sex discrimination rather than expecting a single new statutory definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: §106.11 obligation — address conduct occurring under a recipient's education program or activity
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must address sex-based harassment that occurs 'under any education program or activity' of the recipient, broadly including on a recipient's grounds, during school activities off campus, and under a recipient's disciplinary authority; the provision removes many geographical limitations and recognizes that program-related conduct often occurs off campus or remotely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department emphasizes focusing on whether conduct occurs 'under' the program or activity (i.e., within a context the recipient controls) rather than whether it occurred 'on' or 'off' campus. §106.11 is consistent with recent court decisions and aligns Title IX's scope more closely with Title VII in removing geographic presumptions. Examples include field trips, online classes, athletic programs, and conduct via school-operated electronic systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: §106.11 obligation — address hostile environments even when some contributing conduct occurred outside program or the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient has an obligation to address a sex-based hostile environment under its education program or activity in the United States even when some conduct alleged to be contributing to that hostile environment occurred outside the recipient's education program or activity or outside the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department modified §106.11 wording to clarify that conduct outside the program need not itself be 'sex-based harassment' to be relevant. The recipient's obligation is limited to addressing the hostile environment that exists under its program in the United States; it need not independently respond to alleged conduct that occurred entirely outside the program or outside the United States unless that conduct contributes to a U.S.-based hostile environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hostile-environment factors — totality of the circumstances (five factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating whether a sex-based hostile environment exists, a recipient must evaluate the totality of the circumstances, including: (1) the degree to which the conduct affected the complainant's ability to access the recipient's education program or activity; (2) the type, frequency, and duration of the conduct; (3) the parties' ages, roles within the recipient's education program or activity, previous interactions, and other relevant factors about each party; (4) the location of the conduct and the context in which it occurred; and (5) other sex-based harassment in the recipient's education program or activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all alleged outside conduct will contribute to a hostile environment; recipients must make fact-specific determinations weighing these factors. See discussion in Hostile Environment Sex-Based Harassment—Factors to Be Considered (§106.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibility limited by disciplinary authority/substantial control
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient is responsible for alleged discriminatory conduct only when it exercises disciplinary authority or otherwise has substantial control over the respondent or the context in which the known harassment occurs; a recipient is not responsible for actions of parties over which it lacks significant control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limitation aligns with Davis and related case law: the analysis should focus on the recipient's control over the harasser and the context, not merely on physical location. If the recipient lacks disciplinary authority or substantial control, Title IX liability does not arise under these regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures, law enforcement interaction, and imminent-threat obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient is not required under Title IX to provide supportive measures for off-program conduct that has not contributed to a hostile environment, but nothing prohibits it from doing so; if the recipient has information indicating a specific and imminent threat of sexual assault within its education program or activity, it must take reasonable action (for example, issuing a no-trespass order or notifying law enforcement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may provide counseling or other supportive measures voluntarily. Mandatory reporting laws and concurrent law enforcement proceedings may require different actions; how grievance procedures interact with law enforcement is fact-specific and depends on local laws and procedural requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraterritoriality — Title IX does not apply outside the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department maintains that 20 U.S.C. 1681 does not have extraterritorial application; Title IX applies only 'in the United States' and therefore does not apply to conduct that occurs outside of the United States, including in study abroad programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although Title IX does not apply extraterritorially, a recipient must address a U.S.-based hostile environment that may be informed by conduct abroad. The regulations do not prohibit recipients from addressing conduct occurring abroad under their own codes of conduct or policies, but they are not required by Title IX to address extraterritorial conduct absent its contribution to a U.S.-based hostile environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-exhaustive examples including technology and AI
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct occurring under a recipient's education program or activity may include field trips, online classes, athletic programs, and conduct that takes place via school-sponsored electronic devices, computer and internet networks and digital platforms operated by, or used in the operations of, the recipient, including AI technologies; §106.11's examples are illustrative and not exhaustive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declines to provide an exhaustive list of examples. Whether a particular scenario falls under a recipient's education program or activity is fact-specific and may include additional forms of conduct depending on the facts (e.g., institution-sponsored travel, recipient-recognized organizations' premises).
